sections.description: This section introduces the patient, outlines the key clinical findings, and reviews the initial laboratory and physical examinations that prompted further investigation.
subtopics: Patient demographics, age, BMI, vital signs
Symptoms: polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, glycosuria
Family history of early‑onset diabetes across three generations
Physical exam findings (absence of acanthosis nigricans, blood pressure, heart rate)
Initial biochemical profile: HbA1c, fasting glucose, OGTT results
Lipid profile and its relevance to metabolic syndrome
Screening for diabetic ketoacidosis and other acute complications

sections.description: This section walks the learner through the step‑by‑step reasoning that distinguishes MODY from type 1 and type 2 diabetes, incorporating autoantibody testing, C‑peptide assessment, and clinical probability tools.
subtopics: Key distinguishing features of type 1 diabetes, type 2 diabetes, and MODY
Interpretation of negative GADA and IA‑2A autoantibodies
Glucagon stimulation test: methodology, results, and implications for β‑cell reserve
C‑peptide thresholds for preserved insulin secretion
Use of the Exeter MODY probability calculator and its limitations in non‑White populations
Role of sulfonylurea responsiveness and renal glucose threshold in clinical suspicion
Why initial management with insulin, metformin, and a DPP‑4 inhibitor was reasonable pending genetic results

sections.section_title: 3. Genetic Testing and Pathophysiology of HNF1A‑MODY
sections.description: This section explains the molecular genetics of HNF1A, the process of variant classification, and how the identified novel mutation leads to the observed phenotype.
subtopics: Overview of MODY genetics: inheritance pattern, common genes, prevalence
Structure and function of the HNF1A transcription factor (DNA‑binding vs transactivation domains)
Mechanisms by which HNF1A mutations impair β‑cell function (insulin, GLUT2, pyruvate kinase, SGLT2 expression)
Next‑generation sequencing workflow for MODY panels
Interpretation of the novel c.809A>G (p.N270S) variant using ACMG criteria (population data, computational predictions, segregation)
AlphaMissense scoring and its relevance to pathogenicity
Clinical correlates of DNA‑binding domain mutations versus transactivation domain mutations

sections.section_title: 4. Management Tailored to the Genetic Diagnosis
sections.description: This section details therapeutic decisions made after confirming HNF1A‑MODY, focusing on the rationale for drug selection, dose adjustments, and lifestyle interventions.
subtopics: First‑line pharmacotherapy for HNF1A‑MODY: low‑dose sulfonylureas vs GLP‑1 receptor agonists
Reasons for switching from basal insulin to dulaglutide after genetic confirmation
Evidence base for GLP‑1RA efficacy and hypoglycemia risk in HNF1A‑MODY
Role of metformin and DPP‑4 inhibitors as adjuncts or maintenance therapy
Contraindications: SGLT2 inhibitors in HNF1A‑MODY and risk of dehydration/ketoacidosis
Lifestyle recommendations: diet, exercise, monitoring of glycosuria
Monitoring plan: HbA1c targets, C‑peptide trends, renal function, and microvascular screening

sections.description: The final section reviews the patient’s response to therapy, long‑term surveillance strategy, and broader implications for precision medicine in diabetes.
subtopics: Timeline of glycaemic control: HbA1c reduction from 10.2 % to 6.0 % over 6 months
Discontinuation of insulin and simplification of regimen
Assessment of autonomic dysfunction (sudomotor testing) and its follow‑up
Absence of microalbuminuria and retinopathy at 1‑year follow‑up
Family counseling and cascade genetic testing recommendations
Impact of accurate MODY diagnosis on healthcare costs and quality of life
Future directions: expanding NGS screening, refining ethnicity‑specific MODY calculators, and developing biomarkers to differentiate MODY from common diabetes types
